articles.title: How Yellowstone Became the First National Park
articles.excerpt: The Lower Falls of the Yellowstone River still drop into a deep canyon in northwestern Wyoming. In 1872, while Wyoming was still a territory, Congress reserved the river's headwaters as a public park. President Ulysses S. Grant signed the law on March 1 of that year, creating the world's first national park. Photographs and paintings from Ferdinand V. Hayden's 1871 survey helped make the case in Congress. The Army later guarded the park, and the National Park Service took over the work in 1918.

articles.title: The Eaton Family's Long Ride on Wolf Creek
articles.excerpt: On Wolf Creek, west of Sheridan, the Eaton family has been putting guests on horses for more than a century. Three brothers started a cattle ranch in Dakota Territory in 1879, took paying visitors in 1882, and moved the outfit to the Bighorn slope in 1904. Historians credit Eatons' Ranch as the first dude ranch in the country. The fourth and fifth generations still run the place as a cattle ranch and a guest ranch. The horses still go out in the morning, and the forest is still right over the fence.

articles.title: The Long Fight That Finished Grand Teton National Park
articles.excerpt: The Teton Range rises straight off the Jackson Hole valley floor. The first Grand Teton National Park, created in 1929, stopped at the range and the lakes at the base. A presidential monument in 1943, and a long local fight, followed. Congress in 1950 put most of the valley into a new park. The same act still bars any new national park or monument in Wyoming unless Congress authorizes the change.

articles.title: Wyoming's Official Symbols, Written Into Law
articles.excerpt: The state flag, the Indian paintbrush, the meadowlark, and the bison did not wander into office on their own. The Legislature wrote each symbol into Wyoming law.

articles.title: How Wyoming Became the Equality State
articles.excerpt: Wyoming women won the right to vote in 1869, when this land was still a territory. The name Equality State comes from that law, and from the right later written into the state constitution.

articles.title: A Blue Swing on the High Plains
articles.excerpt: Wyoming had a blue swing from 2024 to 2026. Voters moved toward Democrats in every county. Republicans still won the big races, and one House seat changed parties.

articles.title: Wyoming's 2026 Legislative Election: One Party Flip, 38 Open Seats
articles.excerpt: Unofficial returns show House District 11 moving from Republican to Democratic hands, with 38 open seats.
